newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa's Mandela to send delegation to Zaire.
newsitem.headline: South Africa's Mandela to send delegation to Zaire.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela will send a high-level delegation, possibly led by Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, to Zaire by Monday to try to ensure a democratic transfer of power, an official said.
Presidential spokesman Parks Mankahlana said Mandela had spoken regularly during the past 24 hours to African leaders including Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila.

But he said Mandela had not spoken to President Mobutu Sese Seko, who left the capital for his Gbadolite palace on Friday and announced through a spokesman he would no longer take any active part in the government of Zaire.
Mankahlana said that although Mobutu had not given up the title of president, Mandela regarded his move after 32 years in power as "possibly a positive step".
He said Mandela would ask his representatives to speak to all remaining players including Kabila, the presidential guard, military and members of Mobutu's party and opposition parties.
"The government still sees a role for a kind of transitional arrangement involving all parties in Zaire," he said.

Mandela tried last week to win support from Kabila and Mobutu for a programme for a transition to democracy, including Mobutu's immediate resignation and guarantees of the inclusion of parties other than Kabila's rebel alliance.

South African government sources said Mandela, who ensured a place for opposition parties in his own country after its transition from apartheid in 1994, was anxious to avoid a direct transfer of power from Mobutu to Kabila.

"It seems President Mobutu is out of the picture...but if Kabila just declares himself president, we could simply have another dictatorship," said one source. Kabila on Saturday proclaimed himself head of state as residents of outlying districts of Kinshasa turned out to welcome his forces.

Mankahlana said Mandela would have preferred a constitutional transfer of power, but it might not be necessary for Mobutu to formally resign if other legal means could be found to institute a managed transition.
South African officials on Saturday welcomed U.S. President Bill Clinton's strong statement on Friday that Mandela was leading the Zairean peace initiative and should be supported.
They said Clinton's message could help to avoid a flurry of conflicting international efforts to install democratic structures in Zaire.
